These practices were built with educators, in real schools. Through Marshall's Research-to-Impact work and the IGNITE Network, teachers and leaders tried them, studied what happened, and improved them cycle after cycle. What you will find here is what came through that process: practices specific enough to use on Monday, and honest about what it takes to make them work. Much of this work began in schools serving students too often underserved, with particular attention to students with disabilities and multilingual learners.

IGNITE is a network of schools working together to put strong, evidence-based practices into everyday use. Members test improvements in their own classrooms, share what they are learning, and build the tools that help the next school move faster. The resources on this site come out of that shared work.

Three practice toolkits anchor this site. Co-planning helps general and special educators plan together so every student reaches grade-level work. Repeated reading builds reading fluency through structured, repeated practice. Routine data cycles give teams a regular rhythm for reading student data and adjusting. A fourth section, Leading Implementation, is for the leaders putting this work in place and keeping it going.

It builds on the original Research-to-Impact work with founding charter partners Summit Public Schools, Collegiate Academies, and Green Dot Public Schools, and spreads to new regions through two intermediary partners: the NJ Children's Foundation in Newark, New Jersey, and SCORE (the State Collaborative on Reforming Education) in Tennessee. The independent evaluation is led by Mathematica. This work is supported by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. In partnership with leading researchers, content experts, and educators, Marshall Street developed more than 20 evidence-based practices that improve learning experiences, environments and outcomes for Black and Latinx students with disabilities experiencing poverty. The Research-to-Impact Practices are now available for any school to use.

Schools across America struggle to meet the diverse needs of students, particularly students who face the adverse effects of systemic racism, ableism, and classism. Yet through three years of concentrated effort, 10 public charter school networks across the United States joined together to demonstrate that it is possible to transform teaching and learning for students with disabilities. The collections below document their work and offer a guide for schools committed to creating a more equitable education system. The practices are sorted into five collections by content area.
